neurological_exam.mental_status: Alert and oriented x4. Guarded and hypervigilant. Reports feeling 'checked out' at times.

neurological_exam.gait: Right leg dragging pattern with exaggerated hip hiking; resolves when distracted by conversation.
neurological_exam.additional: Tremor in right hand — variable frequency (4-8 Hz), entrains to tapping rhythm. Episode of staring and unresponsiveness on ward — 90 seconds, eyes closed, not responsive to voice, immediate recovery.

patient.chief_complaint: Right-sided weakness, tremor, and episodes of unresponsiveness — 3 months
patient.history_present_illness: Mr. K is a 31-year-old veteran with combat-related PTSD who presents with a 3-month history of progressive right-sided weakness, right hand tremor, and episodes of unresponsiveness. He served three tours of duty in the Middle East and experienced a blast exposure in 2019 for which he was diagnosed with mild traumatic brain injury. He has been applying for VA disability benefits and his claim was denied 6 weeks ago, which he finds devastating. He is appealing the decision. His neurological symptoms first appeared approximately 3 months ago, shortly after the disability claim process intensified. He initially attributed his symptoms to sequelae of his mild TBI. The episodes of unresponsiveness have been witnessed by his partner: lasting 1-2 minutes, with closed eyes, no limb movements, and immediate full recovery. He has no prior history of seizures. His PTSD symptoms include nightmares, hypervigilance, avoidance, and emotional numbing. He drinks 2-4 beers daily. He acknowledges that his symptoms cause him distress but is resistant to considering a psychological explanation, feeling that this would invalidate his disability claim.

results.title: Functional neurological symptom disorder in veterans: prevalence and relationship to PTSD

output.summary: FND is recognized as a legitimate neurological disorder that frequently co-occurs with PTSD, particularly in combat veterans. VA policy recognizes both PTSD and FND as service-connected conditions when properly documented. The presence of FND does not invalidate a PTSD disability claim — the two conditions are independent diagnoses. FND in veterans with PTSD typically requires integrated treatment addressing both conditions simultaneously.

output.proposed: Naltrexone 50 mg daily (for alcohol use disorder)
warnings: Do not use naltrexone if patient uses opioids — will precipitate withdrawal
Monitor liver enzymes given elevated GGT at baseline
Naltrexone can be used while FND treatment is ongoing — these are parallel treatments

ground_truth.primary_diagnosis: Functional neurological disorder — right-sided functional hemimotor syndrome and PNES, with comorbid PTSD and alcohol use disorder

differential.diagnosis: Chronic traumatic encephalopathy (CTE) from blast TBI
differential.key_feature: Single small microhemorrhage on SWI is not in a location consistent with right-sided motor/sensory deficits; normal formal cognitive testing; CTE does not cause hemiparesis; CTE is a postmortem diagnosis
MRI DWI negative — no acute infarct; inconsistent exam findings with variable strength; positive Hoover sign; patient is 31 years old with no traditional vascular risk factors
Normal NCS — no neuropathy; the right-sided hemibody distribution is inconsistent with alcohol neuropathy which would produce symmetric distal stocking-glove sensory loss
FND is NOT malingering — it is an involuntary neurological disorder; symptoms are real and distressing; should not be presumed based on pending disability claim

optimal_actions.action: MRI brain (with SWI for TBI microhemorrhage assessment)
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Remote TBI microhemorrhage — not causally related to current deficits

optimal_actions.action: Labs including alcohol biomarkers and prolactin
optimal_actions.expected_finding: GGT mildly elevated (alcohol use), prolactin not elevated post-episode

optimal_actions.action: Neuropsychological testing — assess TBI vs FND vs PTSD contribution
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Normal cognitive testing; PTSD symptoms elevated

optimal_actions.action: Psychiatric evaluation — PTSD and alcohol use disorder

critical_actions: Do not attribute current symptoms to remote TBI microhemorrhage (location mismatch)
Avoid implying malingering for disability purposes
Integrated PTSD + FND + alcohol use disorder treatment
VA service connection documentation for FND
contraindicated_actions: Attributing all symptoms to TBI without evidence — remote microhemorrhage is not causally explanatory
Accusing patient of malingering based on disability claim context
key_reasoning_points: Remote TBI microhemorrhage is present but located in right frontal white matter — it cannot explain right-sided hemimotor/hemisensory deficits (would need left hemisphere lesion for right-sided deficit)
Preserved response to pain during 'unresponsive' episode (withdrew hand from sternal rub) is incompatible with true loss of consciousness
FND and PTSD frequently co-occur in veterans — both are legitimate service-connected diagnoses that can coexist
Pending VA disability claim should not bias clinical diagnosis — FND is NOT malingering and occurs regardless of compensation-seeking context

red_herrings.data_point: Remote TBI microhemorrhage on SWI from blast exposure 2019
red_herrings.intended_effect: Attribute all neurological symptoms to TBI sequelae, avoiding FND diagnosis
red_herrings.correct_interpretation: The microhemorrhage location (right frontal) does not explain right-sided hemimotor deficits; formal cognitive testing is normal; symptom pattern requires positive FND signs for diagnosis

metadata.notes: Straightforward FND in veteran with PTSD and remote TBI. Remote microhemorrhage is a red herring. FND and PTSD co-occur and are both valid diagnoses.
